How exactly did we come up with it, what is its use? What concept does it represent? Is it a geometric form, and what formula does it represent?

I'm a total n00b at this, but it seems mighty interesting.

Sorry for the delay, I can try to explain, but first I need to know if you already know what a group is. Or a manifold, Lie group, simple group.

It is no problem if you don't know any of these concepts, but then I would have to start explaining what a group is, why it is important and some examples.

Thank you so much!

I know a bit from engineering, I've seen Euclidean groups, vector space, grid transformations, differential equations, everything that has to do with approximation (boundary conditions, finite elements, Fourier...)

But I've never had a class on abstract algebra, so I'm struggling with group theory. I don't know the math behind a torus for example, only up to 3D.

Ok, lets try it. If I go too fast on some point, please say so.

Lets start with R^3, the usual 3 dimensional real vector space. Take any rotation on R^3 (represent this rotation by A) and some vector u. Now, it will look like a weird notation, but consider the function [A,u] from R^3 back to R^3, given by [A,u] (v)=Av+u. In other words, this function takes a vector v, rotate it by A and them sums it to a fixed vector u. It is a rotation followed by a translation (this type of thing is usually called a rigid motion on R^3). Now, what happens when you have 2 such transformations, say [A,u] and [B,w], and you compose then (i.e., applies you right after another)? For any vector v, you have that [A,u] ([B,w] (v))=[A,u] (Bv+w)=ABv+Aw+u. Note that this is the same as [AB,Aw+u] (v). Now v is any vector, so the composite [A,u][B,w] is [AB,Aw+u] (as A and B are rotations, AB is also a rotation), i.e, the composite of 2 rigid motions is also a rigid motion. More, there is a special rigid motion, [Id,0], where the rotation is the identity map and the translation vector is 0. This motion has the following property: for any other rigid motion [A,u], we have [Id,0][A,u]=[A,u][Id,0]=[A,u]. You also have the following property: given [A,u], let B be the inverse of A, and take the rigid motion [B,-Bu]. Then [A,u][B,-Bu]=[AB,-ABu+u]=[Id,-u+u]=[Id,0]. In a nutshell, there is an operation between rigid motions (the composition), that is associative (didn't show here, it is homework), has a neutral element (an element that when operated with any other element does nothing) and all elements have an inverse (i.e., for any element, there is another element that when operated, gives you the neutral element).

Lets change the subject: pick up the non zero real numbers and consider their product (the usual product, multiplication). The multiplication is associative, for any such number r, r times 1 is r and every such number has associated the number 1/r, such that r times 1/r is 1. In this case, 1 is a neutral element and the inverse of r is 1/r.

Changing the subject again: pick up the integers. There is an associative operation between integers (the sum). If you add zero to any integer, you do nothing. If you pick up any integer a, there is an integer (-a) such that a plus (-a) is zero.

Take all matrices of a given fixed sized, for instance 2x2 matrices. You can sum two such matrices, and the result will also be a 2x2 matrix. This sum is associative. There is a special 2x2 matrix (the matrix whose entries are all 0), called the null matrix. What happens when you sum anything to the null matrix? More, given a matrix A, what happens when you sum A with the matrix -A (the matrix whose entries are the same entries as A, but with reversed signs)?

Again, think of 2x2 matrix, with real entries, but restrict just for the ones that have determinant equal 1. The product (usual matrix multiplication) between 2 such matrix will also have determinant 1. More, this product is associative. The identity matrix (1's on the main diagonal, zero everywhere) have determinant 1 and when you multiply anything by the identity matrix, nothing changes. More: if A has determinant 1, the inverse of A also has determinant 1, and A times its inverse is the identity.

There is a pattern here, and mathematicians like to give patterns names. So, more precisely, a group is a set of objects together with an operation (will denote it by °) between those objects (i.e., a function that has 2 such objects as input and outputs another such object) that has 3 properties:

  1. The operation is associative: for any 3 objects a,b and c, (a°b)°c=a°(b°c) (i.e., operating a with b first, then taking the result and operating with c is the same as operating b with c first and then operating a with the result). Note that the parenthesis changes, but the order of the elements stays the same.

2. There is a special element, called the neutral element, will denote it by n, such that for any element a of the group, a°n=n°a=a.

3. For any element a of the group, there is an element b in the group, called the inverse of a, sometimes denoted by a with superscript -1, such that a°b=b°a=n.

Just with this 3 rules, one can show several things about groups (for instance, there is no other element different from n with the same property as rule 2). Notice that, in general, a°b is not equal b°a (just look at the rigid motions example). When that happens, we say that the group is commutative (or abelian, after the mathematician Abel).

I hope it is clear now why mathematicians like to abstract things: imagine you can show that a certain result is valid just from following the above 3 rules. Then it is valid for any group. So when you are working with, say multiplication of 1000x1000 matrices with determinant 1, you can say "Hey, I don't care that I am working in this specific case, and big matrices are boring and messy to work with. The important thing is that this is a group, so all the results I know are valid for groups are valid here, I just have to take into account what the operation in this specific case is and what the neutral element is!".

There are other examples of groups (permutation groups, symetries of a regular polygon, braid groups...). Group is also just one example of an algebraic structure. You could change the rules and have other weird objects (like for instance, vector spaces) some with weird names, like magma, groupoid, ring, field etc.
